CODE
Art. 2.3.53.
 Contribution 
The spouses may agree that all or part of the present or future movable or real property referred to in Article 2.3.17 shall form part of the common patrimony.
Future spouses who, before entering into marriage, acquire full ownership of a real property may, provided that following such acquisition they are exclusive and equal undivided owners of such property, include a declaration of advance contribution in the deed of acquisition of ownership. By the mere fact of their marriage, the property will then form part of the joint estate, as if they had stipulated the contribution in their matrimonial agreement.
The spouses may derogate from paragraph 1 in their matrimonial agreement.
The notary enters the declaration of advance contribution referred to in paragraph 1 in the central register of matrimonial agreements.
Debts outstanding at the time of the contribution and which have been contracted by the contributing spouse in order to acquire, improve or conserve the contributed property are charged to the joint estate, unless otherwise agreed in the matrimonial agreement or in the declaration referred to in paragraph 2. 
A spouse who has contributed specific property to the joint estate has the right, at the time of the partition, to take back the existing property still in kind by deducting it from his or her share at its value at the time of the partition. This provision does not apply to property contributed jointly by the two spouses.
A spouse who contributes to the common patrimony a specific asset, the value of which is indicated in the matrimonial agreement, may limit his contribution to a certain sum.
Unless otherwise stipulated in the matrimonial agreement, at the dissolution of the regime, he/she is owed by the common patrimony a reward equal to the difference between the value of the property and the sum up to which this property was contributed.
This compensation will be revalued on the basis of the value of the property contributed, either on dissolution of the regime if it is still in the joint estate at that time, or on the date of its alienation if it has been alienated previously; if another property has replaced the alienated property, the compensation is valued on the basis of the value of this new property.
